<meta>This page serves as the introduction to a treatise on astrology, establishing the divine origin of the science and contrasting its ancient glory with modern skepticism.</meta>

# Introduction

Oh! What a unique jewel God has bestowed upon the world in the form of Astrology <note>original: "Jyotish-shastra"</note>, through the influence of which humans can fully understand their past and present deeds and their consequences. In this vast world, every single thing is within the reach of an industrious person. There is no substance that a person of intellectual power cannot know or achieve; only birth and death remain beyond human perception, and it is through this that God’s divinity is revealed. However, Astrology is such a priceless gem that, when its ointment is applied to the eyes, even the hidden mysteries of birth and death become visible. When Lord Brahma <note>The creator deity in Hinduism</note> divided the Vedas into four parts, he established its six limbs: "Phonetics, Ritual, Grammar, Etymology, Prosody, and Astrology." Among these, Astrology is considered the "Crest-Jewel" <note>original: "Shiromani"</note> because of its direct relevance and miraculous nature.

Now, such a time has come that this unique, crowning jewel is falling, stumbling, and being driven away. No one even asks, "Where are you from and who are you?" If by chance someone recognizes it, they insult it, saying: "Yes! You are the same one who, through your miraculous deceptions, lured our ancestors and made them spend all their wealth and physical effort on useless acts of charity and religion, leading them to downfall and making them worthy of our contempt. If they hadn't been caught in your trap, all their earned wealth would have naturally come to us. Why would we have to perform so many kinds of labor for our lifelong sustenance? Now, why should we respect you? If our forefathers were ignorant, so be it; we will never make that mistake. Go away and save your dignity!"

"Moving a little further ahead," another gentleman is encountered. Seeing Astrology, he cries out: "My dear sir! Keep your distance; do not even let your shadow fall upon us! You are inauspicious. I have heard that before our mother's marriage, someone with your 'eye-ointment' <note>A metaphor for astrological insight</note> said that this girl had a 'widowhood yoga' <note>term: "Vaidhavyayoga" — a planetary alignment indicating the early death of a husband</note>. Suddenly, shortly after the marriage, it happened exactly like that. Subsequently, from that very woman with the 'widowhood yoga,' we were born—so healthy and knowledgeable in the scriptures—that we do not even believe a woman can be a widow. All men in the world are portions of God; women never lack for men..."

<summary>The author introduces astrology as a divine "crest-jewel" of the Vedic sciences while lamenting how modern skeptics and those embittered by inheritance or personal tragedy now scorn the practice.</summary>
<keywords>Astrology, Jyotish, Vedas, Brahma, Karma, Skepticism, Widowhood Yoga, Vedangas</keywords>

<page-num>4</page-num>
# Introduction

It is not so. Why should we waste the lives of these poor, helpless women in the state of widowhood? <note>The author is likely responding to a critic who used astrological charts to predict widowhood.</note> Due solely to your harsh words, our mother had to accept widowhood for a few days; but then, by God's grace, such good fortune <note>The term used is 'Saubhagya', implying the auspicious state of a woman whose husband is alive.</note> arose that by its glory, we, such learned scholars, were born into this world. Now tell us! Does our mother possess the yoga <note>A specific planetary alignment or 'union' in a birth chart.</note> of widowhood or of good fortune? You are a liar and your readers are liars! 

Alas, O *Kali Yuga*! <note>The 'Age of Vice' or the current dark age in Hindu cosmology, characterized by spiritual decline.</note> Did you have to exert your authority first upon this wonderful jewel? Was your primary enmity with this alone? Yes, your purpose is clear: if you first attack the crown-jewel of the scriptures, then all others will fall under your sway. However, this eternal scripture <note>Referring to Astrology/Jyotish.</note> will not be easily overcome by your assault even in this state; for a short time, to let the influence of the era manifest, the King of Jewels—Astrology—has withdrawn its wings and is waiting. In the end, a jewel remains a jewel. 

The reason for the current decline in the authority of Astrology is that the predictions made by astrologers do not prove entirely accurate. This is because the King of *Kali* began his entry specifically through the astrologers. The ancient Sages <note>Rishis</note> practiced self-restraint and observances <note>Yama and Niyama</note>, performed penance, were moderate in eating, refused unsolicited gifts, practiced Yoga, were masters of all scriptures, studied the Vedas, and performed the daily fire ritual <note>Agnihotra</note>. Because of this, they could speak of the past, future, and present through *Samadhi*—that is, through one-pointed concentration. 

Now, in place of restraint and observances, astrologers have adopted hypocrisy and greed; instead of moderate eating, they consume meat; instead of refusing gifts, they grab everything; instead of practicing Yoga, they focus on amassing wealth and worldly deception; instead of Vedic study, they perform mere rituals for show; instead of penance and sensory control, they are lustful for women; and in place of the sacred fire ritual, they have tobacco. When the "sages" of today have become like this, how can they possess the intellect required for universal scholarship? Without vast knowledge and without self-control, how can they utter miraculous predictions? 

When those who trade the sacred *Gayatri* mantra—the very essence of a Brahmin—for the sake of priestly fees and accept any gift imaginable, how can their intellect remain pure or their words come true? Even if someone puts in the effort to study and gains some scriptural knowledge, they become filled with vanity and envy. In Astrology, much depends on the guidance of a teacher <note>Guru-lakshya</note>; yet out of envy for another's authority, they ignore those secret methods...

<summary>The author defends the sanctity of Astrology (Jyotish) against the corrupting influence of the Kali Yuga, blaming the inaccuracy of modern predictions on the moral and spiritual decay of contemporary astrologers compared to ancient sages.</summary>
<keywords>Kali Yuga, Astrology, Jyotish, Ethics, Sages, Widowhood, Vedic Rituals, Corruption</keywords>

<header>Introduction</header>

# Introduction

If one considers [knowledge] a secret and does not reveal it to anyone, how can the propagation of science increase in the future? Through such behaviors, this peerless scripture <note>original: "advitiyashastra" — referring here to the unique science of astrology</note> has gradually vanished and reached its current [depleted] state. It is proper for the general public to make every effort toward the advancement of this wonderful jewel. Otherwise, it will be impossible to find such a priceless gem again. Especially, astrologers <term>Jyotishi: practitioners of the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</term> should strive for its advancement, as it is useful for their entire lives, both for the past and the future. 

In this, extreme labor must be put into reading and teaching so that people can provide accurate results that inspire confidence. Look! How much effort the great souls and teachers <note>original: "Mahatma Acharyas"</note> of the past undertook for the welfare and conviction of the general public to propagate this science; yet now, many people say that the science of astrology is nothing, nor do the planets have the power to give good or bad results—that whatever one's karma <note>the sum of a person's actions in this and previous states of existence, viewed as deciding their fate in future existences</note> is, that will surely happen. 

In this situation, some atheists <note>original: "nastik" — those who reject the authority of the Vedas or the existence of a higher order</note> say that the Brahmins <note>the priestly and scholarly class</note> created this entire elaborate deception only for the benefit of their ignorant and lazy offspring. Now, the statement to be made here is that when this "perceptible science" <note>original: "pratyaksha shastra" — a science based on observable phenomena</note> has reached the aforementioned state of decay, it is no surprise that public rumor is such. Nevertheless, they are not aware of the fundamental purpose of this science; otherwise, they would never say such things so hastily. 

The fruit of one's actions <note>original: "karmaphal"</note> must be experienced, but there is no understanding of what that is, or when and what its result will be. Through contemplation of this, the ancient teachers accepted the time of birth as the desired starting point and created such calculations through which that invisible fruit of action becomes visible. They established the names of those calculations as the nine planets <note>The Navagraha: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the two lunar nodes, Rahu and Ketu</note> starting with the Sun, the twelve zodiac signs starting with Aries <note>original: "Meshadi"</note>, and the five limbs of the calendar <term>Panchang: the traditional Hindu calendar based on five temporal elements</term>. These [planets] themselves neither give anything nor can they do anything inauspicious; whatever karma one has earned, the result will be exactly that. However, through the calculation in the form of planets, that which was "unaimed" <note>invisible/unperceivable</note> becomes "aimed" <note>visible/perceivable</note>. 

Now, an illusion has arisen here that if these [planets] are powerless and the fruits must be experienced according to karma, then the worship of planets and giving of charity are also useless. But this superficial view is the "logic of catching a bull by its horns" <note>original: "shringagrahinyaya" — a Sanskrit idiom referring to a direct but simplistic or narrow approach to a complex problem</note>. Its purpose is actually quite sublime: we performed such actions in the past that the result for us is to be misfortune or loss of wealth. This action and its fruit were invisible, but because the period <note>original: "dasha" — a planetary period in astrology</note> of the Sun or some other planet became difficult, the misfortune became known to us. This is a calculation that makes the fruit of karma known...

<summary>The author defends astrology against skeptics and atheists, explaining that planets do not "cause" fate but act as a mathematical system to make invisible past karma visible and predictable.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, karma, Navagraha, Jyotish, skepticism, Panchang, planetary periods, Indian philosophy</keywords>

# Introduction

If we had known beforehand of the actions <note>karma</note> that have now manifested through the Sun, we would have taken measures against them. Since the Sun is the indicator here, we must perform the Vedic-prescribed pacification rites <note>shanti</note> for the Sun as a means of neutralizing that karma. Is this pacification for the Sun itself, or for the accumulated bad karma? Just as the fruits of karma were made known through the Sun, it is appropriate to seek the remedy through the Sun as well. 

In this, there is a twofold benefit. First, there is the pain of suddenly losing wealth that was earned with great effort; if that loss happens by one's own hand through the Sun's planetary period <note>Surya-dasha</note> as a known karmic result, there will be no subsequent regret. The second benefit is that whatever pacification is performed according to Vedic and Scriptural methods will be counted as the neutralization of karma, bringing joy to the mind, rewarding goodness, and being categorized as "righteous expenditure." 

If we do not follow the prescribed methods, the expenditure will be "unrighteous" (wealth that never serves a purpose again) and will cause mental distress at that time—such as money spent on doctors, fines, theft, or losses from fire and floods. In these cases, the fruit of karma is still received. Karma is neutralized through action, and in this, the purification of the mind is primary. <term>Karma-vasana</term> <note>The latent desires or impressions left by past actions</note> even grants rebirth for the sake of experiencing those results. 

Currently, the intellect of the common person is so confused that they believe the body and birth did not exist before and will not exist again; they think the five elements will simply return to their respective places. They ask, "Who takes birth again? No one has ever returned after death to say they were born before or will be born again." This delusion is false. They say "Life" is just the name of the air <note>prana</note>, and it too merges back into the atmosphere. From a physical perspective, nothing remains to take birth, but the fundamental knowledge is this: the impressions <note>vasana</note> of the actions in which the body was engaged remain in seed form. According to those seeds, another manifestation of the five elements is created by the power of those impressions to experience the fruits of karma. There are many proofs for this and much to be said. I intend to write about this subject in greater detail under the pretext of translating some other text.

->“Astrology is the eye of the Veda, Grammar is its ear, Prosody its feet, and Ritual its hands. Just as the crest sits upon the head of a peacock, or the jewel upon the head of a cobra, so does Astrology stand at the head of all the Vedanga sciences.” <note>original: "ज्योतिषामयनं चक्षुर्निरुक्तं श्रोत्रमुच्यते... ज्योतिषं मूर्धानि स्थितम्"</note><-

The first branch of the Vedic eye, the science of Astrology, concerns the fruits of birth...

# Introduction.

I have composed this vernacular commentary on the *Brihat Jataka*—the finest of natal astrology texts—for the easy understanding of children who have seen only a little of the path of <term>Jyotish</term><note>Vedic astrology</note> and lack proficiency in the great <term>Samhita</term><note>Compendiums of omens and mundane astrology</note> texts, as well as to lessen the labor of teachers. Subsequently, a desire arose in me regarding the timing of astrological results, which is often a laborious process. Specifically, when one calculates the <term>Shadbala</term><note>Sixfold strength of planets</note>, <term>Drishti</term><note>Aspects</note>, <term>Baleshta</term><note>Desired strength</note>, <term>Kashtabala</term><note>Affliction strength</note>, and <term>Nisargadi-bala</term><note>Natural and other strengths</note> to determine the <term>Dasha-Antardasha</term><note>Major and minor planetary periods</note>, the traditional Siddhantic methods require great effort only to yield broad timeframes. 

For instance, in the <term>Maheshwari Dasha</term>, Venus lasts 20 years; in the <term>Nisarga Dasha</term>, Saturn lasts 50 years; and when planetary exaltation is full, the Moon’s period is 15 years. Similarly, a minor period (Antardasha) would not be less than 5 or 6 years. If the destiny of the native is fixed, will the result remain exactly the same for that entire 5 or 6-year period? To address this, Lord Surya, the instructor of the eighteen great sages like Brahma, created the <term>Tajika Shastra</term><note>A system of astrology incorporating Persian techniques, focusing on annual solar returns</note>. By calculating the <term>Varshapravesha</term><note>Annual return</note>, <term>Masapravesha</term><note>Monthly return</note>, and even the <term>Dinapravesha</term><note>Daily return</note>, an astrologer can predict results down to the specific day. 

Therefore, after translating the *Brihat Jataka*, I felt it necessary to translate a Tajika text as well. Among Tajika works, the primary one is the *Jirna Tajika*, and its essential summary is the *Neelakanthi*, composed by the scholar Neelakantha Daivajna. Because this text is concise in wording but vast in meaning and widely accepted, I am composing this commentary in the <term>Khari Boli</term><note>The standard dialect of Hindi</note> dialect for the enlightenment of the general public. This is done by the command of the most merciful King of Garhwal, His Highness Maharaja Kirti Shah Bahadur. 

Regarding this <term>Tajika Shastra</term>, some critics cite verses from the <term>Dharmashastra</term><note>Codes of Hindu law and ethics</note> to find fault, such as:

> "One should not speak the Yavana (foreign) language, nor enter a Jain temple, even if being crushed by an elephant or if life is at the very throat." <note>original: "न वदेद्यावनीं भाषां..." This verse warns against adopting foreign customs or non-Vedic religions even in life-threatening situations.</note>

They argue that because this text contains many Persian words like <term>Ikbal</term>, <term>Issaraf</term>, and <term>Itthashala</term><note>Technical terms for planetary configurations in Tajika astrology</note>, it is not fit for Brahmins to study. However, their view is superficial. If the language of other groups were entirely unspeakable, then the <term>Amarakosha</term><note>The celebrated Sanskrit lexicon</note>—the very root of scholarship—would be considered tainted. Furthermore, the eighteen founders of the astrological Samhitas are:

> "Pitamaha, Vyasa, Vashistha, Parashara, Kashyapa, Garga, Marichi, Manu, Angira, Lomasha, Pulastya, Guru (Brihaspati), Shaunaka, and others."

The <term>Jyotish Shastra</term> has proceeded from these sages. Even the *Yavana Jataka* composed by the Greek/Ionian teacher is universally—

<meta>catchword: universally—</meta>

<header>Introduction</header>

# Introduction

This is an authoritative and proven text. The Master of the Greeks <note>original: "Yavanacharya"; referring to the historical transmission of Hellenistic/Persian astrology to India</note> did not rely on his own imagination; rather, he followed the teachings of his predecessors. As stated by Romaka: "That which Brahma told to the Sun, and the Sun told to the Greek, and that which was spoken by the Greek—that is known as Tajika." <note>original: "Brahmana gaditam bhanorbhanuna yavanaya tat..."</note> Furthermore, authorities such as Todarananda, Khut-Khut, Romaka, Hillaj, Vishana, and Durmukhacharya are all masters of Tajika. Since these figures were themselves Brahmins, the use of Persian words in Tajika is not a defect. 

If someone should argue that this contradicts the scriptural injunction "One should not speak the language of the barbarians," <note>original: "Na vadedyavanim bhasham"</note> I have not refuted that law. That verse is indeed true, but its application belongs to subjects like poetic rhetoric. Regarding the use of Persian terms here, the maxim "When the fruit is obtained, what use is the root?" <note>original: "Phale prapte mule kim prayojanam"</note> applies. One's concern is with eating the mango, not with counting the trees. Just as a lotus born from mud is fit for the worship of the gods, and a gem born from the head of a venomous snake is fit for a crown, so too here our concern is with the utility of the science. 

Why hold caste prejudice against a fruitful science? The Tajika system is currently the most effective for revealing results. The Sage Garga has said: "The Greeks are indeed barbarians, but this science is well-established among them. Therefore, they are honored like Rishis; how much more so then a Brahmin who knows the Vedas?" <note>original: "Mlechha hi yavanastheshu..."</note> 

There is also a story in other texts that at one time, astrologers began to challenge the divinity of God by predicting the past, present, and future so accurately. Seeing this, Lord Brahma used the fire of a curse to shroud the miraculous rays of those sciences. In this state, Sages like Vashistha and others made the Tajika system even more miraculous to illuminate their own revealed sciences. The eighteen authors of the Samhitas <note>term: Samhita (encyclopedic collections of astral science)</note> manifested various texts by threading those same Persian words into the jewel-strings of Sanskrit vocabulary. The root of this system also lies in the exact moment of the first breath at birth. I have written extensively on this in the beginning of the "Chapter on Birth" in my *Mahidhari* commentary on the *Brihat Jataka*. 

Now, for the benefit of the public, I have happily surrendered all rights for the publication of this book to Seth Khemraj Shrikrishnadas, the head of the "Shri Venkateshwar" Press.

->Your seeker of grace—the resident of Tehri, the Astrologer Pandit Mahidhar Sharma.<-

# The Tajika Nilakanthi
## With the Vernacular Commentary

---

Having bowed my head with joy and haste to the Supreme Deity—the profound light residing within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus—who is Shiva, the granter of auspiciousness, united with the Goddess <note>original: "Shiva-yutam," referring to Parvati/Shakti</note>, unborn, bathed in nectar, appearing in the form of the Mother and the Guru, and served by all the Bhairavas <note>terrible or fierce forms of Shiva</note>. || 1 || The Brahmin Mahidhara, son of the learned Dharmadatta, having indeed composed a vernacular explanation of the Great Compendium of Nativity <note>The Brihat Jataka, a classic text on birth charts</note>, now extends a beautiful explanation here in the common tongue—called the "Mahidhari"—for the Tajika text named after Nilakantha of the Triganas. || 2 ||

The commentator, for the sake of completing the book without obstacles, describes his own work while offering salutations to the Supreme Brahman in the form of the Guru, Lord Shiva. To the auspicious image, the doer of all good, the one with his power (that is, Shiva with Uma), the self-perfected, sitting with a delighted face bathed in supreme nectar in the most secret, invisible, and imperceptible place within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus; surrounded on all sides by the sixty-four Mothers <note>Matrikas or goddesses</note> and all the Bhairavas—or rather, served by the Mothers as vowels and the Bhairavas as consonants—to that Supreme Deity in the form of the sacred syllable Om <note>Pranava</note> and the Guru-God, I bow my head with excitement and joy. The Brahmin named Mahidhara, son of the wise Dharmadatta, after completing the vernacular commentary on the *Brihat Jataka*, now expands the "Mahidhari" commentary in easy, simple language for the three systems of this astrological treatise, the "Tajika Nilakanthi." || 1 || 2 ||

The author of the original text—the Acharya <term>Acharya: a preceptor or highly learned teacher</term>, the crest-jewel of the lineage of the sage Garga, the crown-gem of all astrologers, the composer of the three-branched <term>Triskandha: the three branches of Jyotish—Siddhanta (astronomy), Samhita (omens), and Hora (horoscopy)</term> astrological treatises, the grandson of the astrologer Chintamani and son of the astrologer Ananta, Sri Nilakantha the Astrologer—being eager to construct the three sections of the ancient Tajika science, namely the System of Definitions <note>Samjna-tantra</note>, the System of Annual Horoscopy <note>Varsha-tantra</note>, and the System of Horary Astrology <note>Prashna-tantra</note>, first begins the first system called the "Discrimination of Definitions"—

<meta>This page continues the introductory section of the Tajika Neelakanthi, a seminal 16th-century Sanskrit treatise on Persian-influenced horoscopy (Tajika Jyotish). This page transitions from the formal invocation to the technical definitions of the zodiac signs.</meta>

# Tajika Neelakanthi

At the beginning, for the completion of the book without obstacles, the author offers salutations to Ganesha, the Sun, and the lotus feet of his father. He then describes the subject, purpose, and connection of the work in the *Upajati* meter:

**Upajati Meter: Having bowed to Ganesha <note>original: "Heramba"</note>, then to the Sun, and likewise to the lotus feet of my teacher Ananta, the illustrious Neelakantha explains through beautiful verses this Tajika system to delight the minds of the learned. || 1 ||**

The astrologer <term>Daivajna: a knower of fate or an astrologer</term> named Neelakantha, having offered obeisance to Ganesha, the Sun-God, and the lotus feet of his father and teacher named Ananta, has studied the ancient Tajika texts. To convey the purpose of those vast volumes through a much shorter work written in beautiful meters like *Indravajra* and *Rathoddhata*, he reveals this "Neelakanthi" Tajika to please the minds of learned astrologers. || 1 ||

**Upajati Meter: Aries is male, movable, fire, a friend, four-footed, blood-red, hot, bilious, loud-voiced, mountain-dwelling, and fierce. It is yellow, strong by day, eastern, rising unevenly, having little sexual contact or offspring, dry, royal, and balanced. || 2 ||**

In the section on terminology <term>Samjna-prakarana</term>, the nature of the zodiac signs is first described. For example—**Aries**: shaped like a ram, a male sign, of "movable" classification, the fire element, strong, four-footed, blood-red in color, and "with heat" meaning a warm body. It is of a bilious temperament <term>Pitta: one of the three Ayurvedic humors associated with fire and digestion</term>, makes a loud sound, wanders in mountains or forests, and has a cruel or fierce nature. It is yellow-colored <insert>[By mentioning both red and yellow here, the combined color of the body is pale red or pinkish]</insert>. It is strong during the day, represents the East direction, engages in little sexual contact, has few offspring, possesses a dry luster, belongs to the Warrior <note>Kshatriya</note> caste, and is "odd" in the numerical counting of signs, yet it provides "even" or balanced results in its effects; for this reason, these qualities are attributed to Aries. || 2 ||

**Upajati Meter: Taurus is fixed, female, earth, cool, dry, desiring the south, good land, windy, nocturnal, and four-footed. It is white, very loud, rising unevenly, with moderate offspring and contact, auspicious, and of the merchant class. || 3 ||**

**Taurus**: shaped like a bull, of "fixed" classification, a female sign, the earth element, dry luster, cool nature, and represents the South direction. It dwells on level ground, is of a windy temperament <term>Vata: the Ayurvedic humor associated with air and movement</term>, and is strong at night. It has four feet, is white in color, makes a loud sound, and has an uneven rise. It is neither excessively lustful nor lacking in desire, is a gentle sign, belongs to the Merchant <note>Vaishya</note> caste, and has a firm, strong body. These are the characteristics of the sign Taurus. || 3 ||

### **Indravajra Meter—The West-wind, parrot-colored, two-footed, a couple, dual-bodied, odd, day-strong, and hot.**
### **Moderate in procreation and mating, forest-dwelling, Shudra by caste, long-voiced, oily, day-strong, and fierce. || 4 ||**

<note>The Sanskrit verse above is in the Indravajra meter, a classical poetic structure.</note>
A pair consisting of one woman and one man is called Gemini <note>original: "Mithun"</note>; such is its form. The characteristics of the Gemini sign are as follows: it is the ruler of the western direction, of the air element <note>original: "Vayutattva"</note> (airy temperament), green-colored like a parrot, two-footed, gentle, male in form, and of a dual nature <note>original: "Dvisvabhava"</note>—the first half is fixed and the second half is movable. It is an odd-numbered sign, hot in nature, moderate in sexual union, with very few offspring. It is a forest-dweller, of the Shudra caste, possesses a long voice, an oily (smooth) body, is powerful during the day, designated as "cruel" or fierce, and has a firm body. || 4 ||

**Upendravajra Meter—Abundant in mating and offspring, the Crab is a wanderer, feminine, pale-pink, and voiceless. ||**
**Auspicious, phlegmatic, oily, water-dwelling, rising evenly, Brahmin by caste, and ruler of the Night and the North. || 5 ||**

The characteristics of Cancer <note>original: "Kark"</note> are as follows: it is shaped like a crab, highly inclined toward mating, many-footed, a movable sign, and of the female gender. Its color is "Patala," meaning pale-pink or whitish. It is voiceless (silent), gentle, of a phlegmatic temperament <note>original: "Kapha"</note>, with an oily body. It belongs to the water element <note>original: "Jaltattva"</note>, is a water-dweller, designated as "even," of the Brahmin caste, powerful at night, the ruler of the northern direction, and possesses a firm body. || 5 ||

**Upajati Meter—Male, fixed, fire, day-strong, bilious, and dry; yellow, hot, ruler of the East, firm, and four-footed. ||**
**Rising evenly, long-voiced, little mating or offspring; the Lion dwells on mountains, a king, fierce and smoke-colored. || 6 ||**

The characteristics of Leo <note>original: "Simha"</note> are as follows: it is shaped like a lion and is male. It is a fixed sign, of the fire element <note>original: "Agnitattva"</note>, powerful during the day, of a bilious temperament <note>original: "Pitta"</note>, and has a dry body. It is yellow in color, hot in nature, the ruler of the eastern direction, and has strong limbs. It is four-footed, designated as "even," has a long voice, is less inclined toward mating, and has few offspring. It is a mountain-dweller, of the kingly (Kshatriya) class, and is smoke-colored <note>original: "Dhumra"</note>. Here too, two colors are mentioned; the purpose is the same as with Aries—the first half is yellow and the second half is the color of smoke. || 6 ||

**Upajati Meter—Pale, two-footed, a woman, dual-natured, ruler of the South, night-strong, airy, cool, rising evenly, and of the earth. ||**
**The Maiden is half-voiced, auspicious, a dweller of the land, Vaishya by caste, dry, with little mating or offspring, and beautiful. || 7 ||**

The characteristics of Virgo <note>original: "Kanya"</note> are: the form of a young maiden, pale (yellowish-white) in color, two-footed, a female sign, and of a dual nature (like Gemini).

## <note>Upajati meter</note> -- Capricorn has the face of a deer, seeks wealth, rules the southern quarter, is feminine, tawny, and harsh. It dwells on auspicious ground and is cold in nature. It has few offspring, is associated with the wind, and is strong at night. Its first half is four-footed, it rises unevenly, and belongs to the merchant class. || 11 ||

It is gentle, a land-dweller, cold by nature, has little contact with women, and few offspring. It is of the air element <note>The Sanskrit verse mentions earth, while the commentary notes air; in standard astrology, Capricorn is Earth</note>, strong at night, the first half is a four-footed animal and the second half is a water-dweller. ## <note>Upajati meter</note> -- Aquarius is footless, a man, strong in the middle of the day, and stable. It is variegated, dwells in the forest, and is of the air. It is smooth, hot, has broken voice, and balanced humors. It is of the servant class, rules the west, and rises unevenly. || 12 ||

<page-num>6</page-num>
# Tajika Nilakanthi
<note>A classic 16th-century Sanskrit treatise on Tajika astrology, which incorporates Perso-Arabic influences into Indian systems.</note>

The purposes of the previously mentioned elements are now explained: the compatibility of elements and categories should be considered in the matching of a man and woman, a master and servant, or a teacher and student. For instance, there is a natural affinity between the Earth element and the Water element, as well as between Fire and Air. Conversely, Earth and Fire, or Water and Air, are mutually inimical. In the aforementioned relationships, if the zodiac signs of both parties belong to the same element, there is greater affection. The latter half of Sagittarius is a quadruped <note>four-legged</note> while the first half is a biped <note>two-legged</note>. The latter half of Capricorn is a legless aquatic creature, while the first half is a bipedal land-dweller. || 14 ||

->**Indravajra Meter**—Bile, wind, balanced humors, and phlegm are to be understood by the learned in groups of three starting from Aries. The Warrior, Merchant, Laborer, and Priest classes likewise follow this order; all results should be determined according to the nature of the zodiac signs. || 15 ||<-
<note>original: "पित्तानिलौ धातुसमः कफश्च..." This verse is written in the Indravajra poetic meter.</note>

The method for calculating the bodily humors and social classes is explained in a simple manner: the humors—Bile <term>Pitta: the fire/metabolic force</term>, Wind <term>Vata/Anila: the air/movement force</term>, Balanced <note>a mix of all three</note>, and Phlegm <term>Kapha: the water/structural force</term>—should be known by rotating through the signs starting from Aries in three cycles. For example:
*   **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius:** Biliary temperament.
*   **Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn:** Windy temperament.
*   **Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius:** Balanced temperament (a combination of wind, bile, and phlegm).
*   **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces:** Phlegmatic temperament.

Social classes <term>Varna</term> are identified in the same sequence:
*   **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius:** Warrior class <term>Kshatriya</term>.
*   **Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn:** Merchant class <term>Vaishya</term>.
*   **Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius:** Laborer class <term>Shudra</term>.
*   **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces:** Priestly class <term>Brahmin</term>.

Whatever qualities, classes, or humors have been ascribed to the signs should be applied when interpreting a birth chart, a yearly solar return, or a divinatory question. One should predict results based on these names: for example, a "cruel" sign indicates a harsh nature, a "gentle" sign indicates a mild nature, a "movable" sign indicates changeability, a "fixed" sign indicates stability, and a "dual-natured" sign indicates a mix of both. Thus, all qualities of the signs should be applied with intelligence to births, years, and questions; the scriptures are merely an aid to one's own intellect. A more detailed expansion of these sign qualities is written clearly in the *Mahidhari* commentary of the *Brihat Jataka* <note>A foundational 6th-century text on Indian astronomy and astrology</note>. || 15 ||

# Tajakaneelakanthi
## Page 8

Divide by 7 and place the <term>quotient</term> (the result of division) along with its own <term>one-fourth part</term> in the second position of the sum. Multiply the remainder by 60 and divide by 40; place this <term>quotient</term> in the third position. These three figures represent the Day, <term>Ghati</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>, and <term>Pala</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 seconds</note>. To these, add the birth day and the desired <term>Ghati</term> and <term>Pala</term> in their respective order. If the <term>Ghati</term> or <term>Pala</term> exceed 60, subtract 60 and add the <term>quotient</term> to the unit above it. If the sum of the days (including the <term>elapsed years</term> plus their <term>one-fourth part</term>) is greater than 7, divide by 7 and take the remainder. Another method for this is described as:

-> "One and a quarter, then half, then one and a half" <-

Or (Year plus a quarter, half, and one and a half). This means: take the <term>elapsed years</term> and add a quarter to find the Day; then take "half" of the years to find the <term>Ghatika</term>; then take "one and a half" times that to find the <term>Pala</term>. When the birth day and desired <term>Ghati-Pala</term> are added in order, the result is the <term>constant</term> (Dhruvaka) Day, <term>Ghati</term>, and <term>Pala</term> for the year. 

**Example:** Following the method of the first verse—suppose the birth <term>Samvat</term> <note>The Vikrami Era calendar</note> 1906 is subtracted from the <term>Year Entry</term> <term>Samvat</term> 1943; the remainder is 37. Similarly, subtracting the birth <term>Shaka</term> <note>The Shaka Era calendar</note> 1771 from the current <term>Shaka</term> 1808 leaves 37 <term>elapsed years</term>. Adding its one-fourth part (9 | 15) results in 46 Days and 15 <term>Ghati</term>. Next, the <term>elapsed years</term> (37) are multiplied by 21, resulting in 777. Dividing this by 40 gives a <term>quotient</term> of 19 <term>Ghati</term>. Adding this to the 15 <term>Ghatika</term> below the 46 Days results in 34 <term>Ghati</term>. The remainder is multiplied by 60 and divided by 40, yielding a <term>quotient</term> of 25 <term>Pala</term> and 30 <term>Vi-pala</term> <note>1/60th of a Pala</note>. Adding the birth data (Day 2 | 39 | 29) to these gives the year's start time.

The second method is: <term>Elapsed years</term> plus a quarter is 46 Days 15 Ghati. Half of the <term>elapsed years</term> is 18 Ghati 30 Pala. One and a half times the <term>elapsed years</term> is 55 Pala 30 Vi-pala. Adding these all to their respective categories: the <term>Vi-pala</term> remains 30; adding 30 and 55 <term>Pala</term> gives 85, which divided by 60 leaves 25 <term>Pala</term> and a <term>quotient</term> of 1 <term>Ghati</term>. Adding the <term>Ghati</term> (1 + 18 + 15) gives 34 <term>Ghati</term>. Adding the birth day (2) and time (39 Ghati 29 Pala) to these (46 | 34 | 25 | 30) results in Day 7, 13 <term>Ghati</term>, 54 <term>Pala</term>, and 30 <term>Vi-pala</term>. This is the <term>Year-Desired</term> (Varsheshta) time. Another method involves multiplying the <term>elapsed years</term> separately by 1 | 15 | 31 | 30. This also yields the <term>constant</term> Day and time. There are many other methods; the rationale for this is that the Sun's full 12...

->Included with the Language Commentary<-

One <term>Solar Year</term><note>Sauravarsha: the time it takes for the Sun to return to the exact same longitudinal position in the zodiac</note> is completed when the Sun returns to the same zodiacal sign and degree it occupied at the moment of birth. The exact time when the Sun reaches those precise coordinates is the moment of the <term>Yearly Entrance</term><note>Varshapravesha: the commencement of the new astrological year for an individual</note>. Based on <term>Civil Days</term><note>Savana: a day measured from sunrise to sunrise</note>, the Sun returns to that same position in 365 days, 15 <term>Ghatis</term>, 31 <term>Palas</term>, and 30 <term>Vipalas</term><note>Traditional Indian units of time: 1 Ghati = 24 minutes; 1 Pala = 24 seconds; 1 Vipala = 0.4 seconds</note>. This value is fixed as the <term>Constant</term><note>Kshepaka</note>. By multiplying this constant across the four units of time by the number of <term>Elapsed Years</term><note>Gatavarsha</note> and carrying over the full units to the next higher denomination, the total civil time elapsed for that age is found. 

For example: Multiply 1, 15, 31, and 30 by 37 elapsed years. This results in 37, 555, 1147, and 1110. By dividing these by the standard 60 (for Ghatis, Palas, and Vipalas), we find that 37 years, 46 days, 34 Ghatis, 25 Palas, and 30 Vipalas have passed in civil time. This method should be understood for all such calculations. By adding the weekday of birth to these 46 days (and subsequent units), the specific weekday and time of the Yearly Entrance is determined. || 16 ||

->**Anushtup Meter**<-
->The elapsed years multiplied by eleven, increased by a fraction of one-one hundred and seventieth, then divided by thirty; add the birth lunar day to the remainder to find the lunar day of the Yearly Entrance. || 17 ||<-
<note>original: "शिवघ्नोऽब्द: स्वखाद्रींदुलवाढ्य: स्वाग्निशेषितः ॥ जन्मतिथ्यन्वितस्तत्र तिथ्यावब्दप्रवेशनम् ॥ १७ ॥"</note>

Once the weekday of the Yearly Entrance is known by the previous method, the following process is used to find the specific <term>Lunar Day</term><note>Tithi</note> on which this entrance occurs: Multiply the elapsed years by 11. Place this result in two positions. In the first position, divide by 170 and add the resulting quotient to the second position. Then, divide that total by 30. To the remainder, add the birth lunar day (counting from the first day of the bright fortnight). This gives the lunar day of the Yearly Entrance. 

**Example:** Multiply 37 elapsed years by 11 to get 407. Place this in two spots. Divide 407 by 170 to get a quotient of 2. Add this 2 to the other 407 to get 409. Add the birth lunar day (9th) to get 418. Divide by 30; the remainder is 28. This indicates the Yearly Entrance occurs on the 28th lunar day, which is the 13th day of the dark fortnight <insert>Krishna Trayodashi</insert>. 

In this calculation, the lunar day might occasionally shift by one day forward or backward. The correct day is the one where the calculated weekday matches either the day before, the day after, or the calculated lunar day itself. Here, the weekday is the primary factor; the lunar day is used to confirm which specific occurrence of that weekday within the month is the correct one, as a weekday repeats 4 or 5 times a month. In this example, the 28th lunar day was found, and the Yearly Entrance occurred on Saturday, the 12th lunar day...

# Tajika Neelakanthi

<page-num>10</page-num>
->Tajika Neelakanthi<-

The solar return <note>The exact moment the Sun returns to its birth position</note> occurs when the Sun reaches the same degree as at birth. Alternatively, the day of the solar return is determined when the weekday matches the day the Sun reaches that specific degree. In some regions, the day of the *Sankranti* <note>The Sun's entry into a new zodiac sign</note> is used for calculation; these are referred to as *Gata* (past) and *Pravishtha* (entered). The day is confirmed if the required weekday falls on that *Pravishtha* day or one day before or after it. || 17 ||

> *Translation of Verse 18:* Multiply the daily motion of the planet by the number of days elapsed or remaining, then divide by sixty. The resulting degrees and minutes should be subtracted or added to make the planetary position accurate. || 18 ||

The accuracy of astrological predictions depends on the precise position of the planets. Calculating this through the primary astronomical treatises (*Siddhantas*) or shorter manuals like *Grahalaghava* involves great labor. Here, the Teacher has provided an easy method for clarifying planetary positions: multiply the daily motion found in the almanac (*Panchang*) by the time elapsed from the reference point to the desired moment, then adjust the reference position accordingly. 

**Example:** The solar return occurs in the year 1886 <note>Samvat 1943</note> on the 12th day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vaishakha, a Saturday, at 13 *ghatis* and 54 *palas* <note>Traditional units of time; 1 ghati = 24 minutes</note>. The almanac provides the planetary positions for the morning of the 8th day of the dark fortnight of Vaishakha (a Monday). The time elapsed from that reference morning to the desired moment is 5 days, 13 *ghatis*, and 54 *palas*. Since this time is yet to come from the reference point, it is called *Aishya* (future/remaining). 

The Sun's position at the reference point was 0 signs, 13 degrees, 37 minutes, and 52 seconds, and its daily motion was 58 minutes and 14 seconds. Multiplying the motion by the elapsed time (5 days, 13 *ghatis*, 54 *palas*) using the *Gomutrika* <note>A "zigzag" or "cow-path" method of multiplication used in ancient Indian mathematics</note> or fractional multiplication method results in 5 degrees, 4 minutes, and 39 seconds. Since the desired time is after the reference point, we add this to the reference position (0s 13° 37' 52"). The resulting sum, 0s 18° 42' 31", is the precise position of the Sun for that moment. This same method should be applied to Mars and all other planets.

Another method to clarify planetary positions using only the almanac's "planetary motion tables" (*Graha Chalaka*) without a reference position is as follows: find the difference between the planetary motion value at the beginning of the constellation quarter (*Nakshatra Charana*) prior to the solar return and the value at the end. Use the Rule of Three <note>A mathematical proportion: if A gives B, what does C give?</note> to calculate: if a certain number of days results in a movement of 3 degrees and 20 minutes <note>The span of one Nakshatra quarter</note>, how much movement occurs in the interval from the first motion value to the desired time? Add the result to the total degrees already completed by the planet in its respective constellation quarters.

<page-num>11</page-num>
->With Language Commentary<-

To the extent that the previous calculation for the desired day and time is found, the elapsed result from the <term>Rule of Three</term><note>A mathematical method (proportions) to find an unknown fourth value from three known values.</note> should be added to that time; this makes it "clear" or accurate.

The main thing to remember here is that one Zodiac sign consists of 9 quarters of the <term>Nakshatras</term><note>Lunar mansions or star clusters used in Vedic astrology.</note>. The movement through one quarter of a Nakshatra is exactly 3 degrees and 20 minutes. Thus:
* 6 degrees 40 minutes for two quarters
* 10 degrees 0 minutes for three quarters
* 13 degrees 20 minutes for four quarters
* 16 degrees 40 minutes for five quarters
* 20 degrees 0 minutes for six quarters
* 23 degrees 20 minutes for seven quarters
* 26 degrees 40 minutes for eight quarters
* 30 degrees 0 minutes for nine quarters are completed.

This is also the sequence for the <term>Navamsha</term><note>The ninth part of a sign, a crucial sub-chart in Indian astrology.</note>. One quarter, or 3 degrees 20 minutes, equals 200 minutes of arc. All these figures are used in the Rule of Three.

**Example:** The solar return (year-entry) occurs in the year 1897 <note>Samyat 1954</note>, on the 12th day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vaishakha, Saturday, at 13 <term>Ghatis</term> and 54 <term>Pals</term><note>Traditional units of time: 1 Ghati = 24 minutes; 1 Pal = 24 seconds.</note>. On the previous day, Friday, at 41 Ghatis and 46 Pals, the calculation was at the third quarter of the Revati star. On Monday, the 14th day, at 53 Ghatis and 3 Pals, the calculation is at the fourth quarter of Revati. The difference between these is 3 days, 11 Ghatis, and 17 Pals. From the first calculation to the desired time, the difference is 0 days, 32 Ghatis, and 8 Pals.

Now the Rule of Three is: if a movement of 3 degrees 20 minutes occurs in a time difference of 3 days 11 Ghatis 17 Pals, then how much will occur in a time difference of 0 days 32 Ghatis 8 Pals? One must multiply 3 degrees 20 minutes by 0 days 32 Ghatis 8 Pals and divide by 3 days 11 Ghatis 17 Pals. The process of multiplication and division follows the <term>Gomutrika</term><note>Literally "cow's urine path"; a zig-zag method of multiplication used in ancient Indian mathematics.</note> and fraction methods.

For easy understanding, the method is as follows: multiply 3 degrees by 60 and add 20 minutes; the total "body" of the multiplier becomes 200 minutes. For the second amount, 0 days 32 Ghatis 8 Pals: if there were a number in the place of zero, we would multiply by 60 and add 32, but here 32 is simply added to zero. Now, multiplying 32 by 60 gives 1920; adding 8 gives 1928 as the multiplier. Multiplying the two values together results in 385,600. This is divided by the "body" of 3 days 11 Ghatis 17 Pals, which is 11,477. The result is 33 minutes. By multiplying the remainder by 60 and dividing by the divisor, the quotient would be degrees and the remainder minutes. Here, 33 is less than sixty, so it remains as minutes, and degrees are 0. Now, consider that in the third quarter of Revati, 0 degrees 33 minutes 36 seconds...

# Tajika Neelakanthi

<page-num>12</page-num>

->Tajika Neelakanthi<-

The calculation for the **True Mercury** <note>original: "Spashta Budha"; the mathematically corrected position of the planet</note> was completed. Before this, one quarter of the constellation Purva Bhadrapada, four quarters of Uttara Bhadrapada, and two quarters of Revati—totaling seven quarters—were passed, resulting in 23 degrees and 20 minutes. Now, adding the 0 degrees, 33 minutes, and 36 seconds calculated by proportion for the third quarter of Revati, the True position becomes 23 degrees, 53 minutes, and 36 seconds. Since Mercury is in the sign of Pisces, it is appropriate to write 11 in the place of the Zodiac Sign <note>In Vedic astrology, Pisces is the 12th sign, represented by the number 11 as it follows 11 completed signs</note>. Thus, 11s 23° 53' 36" becomes the instantaneous True position of Mercury. One should understand the method for others in this same way. These two methods have been described in a simplified manner for the sake of ease. While they suffice for general work, precise calculations are performed using astronomical tables <term>Karana-sarani; simplified astronomical manuals</term> such as *Grahalaghava*, *Mahadevi*, *Makaranda*, and *Ramavinoda*. Even more precise results come from the *Siddhantas* <term>comprehensive theoretical treatises on astronomy</term>. The method for calculating the **True Moon** is similar, as follows:

> **Bhujangaprayatam Meter** <note>A poetic meter consisting of four 'Yagana' feet</note>—Multiply the elapsed portion of the constellation by sixty and divide by the total duration. Multiply the number of elapsed constellations by sixty and add the previous result. Multiply this by two and divide by nine to find the degrees. To find the daily motion, divide 48,800 by the total duration of the constellation. || 19 ||

On the day the True Moon is to be calculated, one must determine the elapsed time <term>Bhukta</term>, the remaining time <term>Bhogya</term>, and the total duration <term>Sarva Bhogya/Bhabhoga</term> of the constellation <term>Nakshatra</term> at the desired time. The method is this: the number of *ghatis* and *palas* <note>traditional units of time; 1 ghati = 24 minutes</note> the constellation has passed until the desired time is called the 'elapsed'. What remains is the 'to be passed', and the sum of both is the 'total duration'. Multiply the elapsed time by 60 and divide by the total duration; the result is the elapsed portion in a 60-unit scale. Count the number of constellations passed from Ashwini onwards, multiply that number by 60, and add the *ghatis* obtained from the current constellation's duration. This gives the total elapsed *ghatis*. Then, multiply by 2 and divide by 9; the quotient is the degrees. Multiply the remainder by 60 and divide by 9 to get the minutes <term>Kala</term>. Again, multiply the remainder by 60 and divide by 9 to get the seconds <term>Vikala</term>. If the degrees exceed 30, divide by 30; the quotient is the Zodiac Sign and the remainder is the degrees. This completes the calculation of the True Moon.

**Example:** Year 1943 of the Vikram Era, month of Vaishakha, dark fortnight, 12th day, Saturday. At the desired time of 13 *ghatis* and 54 *palas*, the elapsed time of the constellation Uttara Bhadrapada is 54 *ghatis* and 13 *palas*...

# Tajika Nilakanthi

The result obtained by division is the <term>Spashta-gati</term> <note>true daily motion</note> of the Moon. **Example:** To divide 48,000 by the total remaining portion of the Nakshatra Uttara Bhadrapada (64 minutes, 54 seconds), first convert the divisor into seconds (3894). > *Upajati Meter*—The half-duration of the day or night, minus the elapsed time of day or night, is the **Eastern Nata**. Conversely, the elapsed time of day or night minus the half-duration is the **Western Nata**. || 20 ||
<note>original: "पूर्व नतं स्याद्दिनरात्रिखंडं..."</note>

After calculating the true positions of the planets, it is necessary to determine the house divisions (<term>Bhava Spashta</term>). Since the houses are derived from the Ascendant and the Midheaven (10th house), we first describe the calculation of <term>Nata</term> <note>hour angle or distance from the meridian</note> to find the Midheaven. 

**Eastern Nata** of the day occurs from midnight until midday. **Western Nata** of the day occurs from midday until sunset. For the night, **Eastern Nata** lasts from sunset until midnight, and **Western Nata** lasts from midnight until sunrise. 

If the desired time (<term>Ishtakala</term>) is before noon, subtract the desired time from the midday point (half-day duration); the remainder is the **Day Eastern Nata**. If the desired time is after noon but before sunset, subtract the midday point from the desired time; the remainder is the **Day Western Nata**. If the desired time is after sunset but before midnight, subtract the desired time from the midnight point (half-night duration); the remainder is the **Night Eastern Nata**. If the desired time is after midnight but before sunrise, subtract the midnight point from the desired time; the remainder is the **Night Western Nata**. 

Note: Subtracting the *Nata* from 15 <note>the standard 6-hour quadrant in Indian time units</note> gives the *Unnata* (altitude), but since *Unnata* is not required here, it has not been detailed. These *Nata* values will be used to calculate the 10th house. 

**Example:** Here, the desired time is 13 *ghatis* and 54 *palas*. The midday point is 16 *ghatis* and 31 *palas*. Subtracting the desired time from the midday point leaves 2 *ghatis* and 37 *palas*. This is the **Day Eastern Nata**. || 20 ||

> ...from the past and future movements of their own rising. Multiply the remainder by thirty and divide by the "impure" <note>original: "ashuddha" - referring to the divisor in the calculation</note> to find the degrees and so on. ||22|| In the difference between the impure and pure, subtract or add the degrees of the precession of the equinoxes. Add the degrees of the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayanamsha: the longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</term> to the instantaneous clear position of the Sun. The sign following the resulting sign is its own rising <note>the zodiac sign currently rising on the horizon</note>. The remaining degrees and so on are considered "elapsed" <term>Bhukta: the portion of the sign already passed</term>. By subtracting these from thirty, the "remaining" portions <term>Bhogya: the portion of the sign yet to rise</term> are found. 

Multiply these remaining or elapsed portions in three separate places by the local rising-interval <term>Lagnakhanda: the time it takes for a specific zodiac sign to rise at a particular latitude</term> of that same sign and divide by thirty. The resulting units in <term>Pala: a unit of time equal to 24 seconds</term> are the elapsed or remaining portions of the Sun. That is, if you multiply the elapsed degrees by the rising-interval, the result of the division by thirty is called "elapsed"; if done with the remaining degrees, it is called "remaining." 

Subtract these palas from the desired time <note>Ishta Ghati: the specific time since sunrise for which the chart is being cast</note> converted into palas. From the remainder, continue subtracting the subsequent rising-intervals one by one. The rising-interval that cannot be subtracted is designated as "impure" <note>Ashuddha</note>. Multiply the remainder of that subtraction by thirty and divide by that "impure" rising-interval; the result is in degrees and so on. Place the number of signs corresponding to the rising-intervals previously subtracted before these resulting degrees. This is the sequence for the "remaining" method. In the "elapsed" method, subtract from the impure and then subtract the precession of the equinoxes; this results in the clear Ascendant <term>Lagna Spashta: the exact longitude of the rising sign</term>.

**Example:** Samvat 1943, Vaisakha Krishna Dwadashi, Saturday. Desired time: 13 Ghatis, 54 Palas. Clear Sun: 0s 18° 42' 31". Added precession <note>Ayanamsha</note>: 22° 44'. The result is 1s 11° 26' 31"; this is the Tropical <note>Sayana</note> Sun. Here, the 1 sign indicates Taurus is the rising sign. The remaining degrees etc., 11° 26' 31", are "elapsed." Subtracting from thirty gives 18° 33' 29" as the "remaining" degrees. 

Now these must be multiplied by the rising-interval segments. The method for rising-intervals is as follows: the rising times at the equator <note>Lankodaya</note> are 278, 299, and 323 in order, and 323, 299, 278 in reverse order. To these, add the ascensional difference segments <term>Chara-khanda</term> of the desired location in one sequence and subtract them in the other to find the local rising-intervals. For example, the equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha</term> of Srinagar is 7.0 (multiplied by three and ten by the serpents— <note>The text cuts off here, likely referencing a mnemonic verse for calculation</note>

# Page 17
## With Commentary in the Common Tongue

The Sun’s instantaneous <term>Sayana</term><note>The tropical longitude of the Sun, adjusted for the precession of the equinoxes.</note> position is multiplied by its own rising period. The portions already traversed (elapsed) and those yet to be traversed (remaining) are calculated using the "subtraction method." By converting these into <term>Palas</term><note>A traditional unit of time; 60 Palas equal 1 Ghatika (24 minutes), and 1 Pala equals 24 seconds.</note>, the precise position of the Sun is determined. This is then subtracted from the desired time (the <term>Ishtakala</term>) expressed in Palas. In this context, the "inclination" (zenith distance) or "elevation" is treated as the desired time. By following the same procedure as used for calculating the Ascendant (<term>Lagna</term>), the Tenth House (<term>Dasham Lagna</term>) is clarified.

For example: just as the instantaneous position of the Sun was taken to clarify the Ascendant, the same is taken here. By multiplying the elapsed degrees by the rising sign's specific value and dividing by thirty, the resulting Palas belong to the Sun. Subsequently, the "elevation Palas" (treated as the desired time) are reduced by these solar Palas. Then, the rising sign values are subtracted; if they cannot be subtracted further, the remaining Palas are multiplied by thirty and divided by the previous "impure" rising sign value. The quotient gives the degrees and minutes. By subtracting these from the sign and further subtracting the <term>Ayanamsha</term><note>The value representing the shift between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs.</note>, the precise longitude of the Tenth House is obtained. This is the "subtraction method" (<term>Rina</term>).

Alternatively, in the "addition method" (<term>Dhana</term>), the degrees of the Sun's instantaneous position are subtracted from 30 and multiplied by the rising period. Dividing by 30 gives the "remaining" (<term>Bhogya</term>) Palas of the Sun. This is subtracted from the western inclination (the desired time). If it cannot be subtracted, the remainder is multiplied by 30 and divided by the "impure" rising sign value. The resulting degrees and signs are added in sequence, and the Ayanamsha is subtracted. Thus, the Tenth House longitude is clarified.

Once the Ascendant and the Tenth House are clarified, adding six signs to the Ascendant clarifies the Seventh House. Thus, four primary houses (the <term>Kendras</term> or Angles) are clarified.

The method for the <term>Bhava Sandhis</term><note>The "junctions" or cusps between two astrological houses.</note> is as follows: subtract the Ascendant from the Fourth House. Divide the remainder by six to obtain the "sixth part" (<term>Shashtamsha</term>). Adding this sixth part to the Ascendant gives the junction between the First and Second houses. Adding it again gives the Second House. Adding it to the Second House gives the junction between the Second and Third houses. Adding it again gives the Third House, and adding it once more gives the junction between the Third and Fourth houses. Adding it to that junction will result in the Fourth House (which was originally created by adding six signs to the Tenth House).

Next, subtract the previously calculated "sixth part" from one full sign (30 degrees). The resulting value (the <term>Kshapaka</term>) is added to the Fourth House to find the junction between the Fourth and Fifth houses. Adding it again gives the Fifth House, and adding it to that gives the junction between the Fifth and Sixth houses; adding it once more gives the Sixth House.

# Tajika Neelakanthi

By adding [six signs] to this, the Seventh House is obtained, which is exactly six signs away from the Ascendant <note>The 'Lagna' or the point rising on the eastern horizon</note>. Now, continue adding six signs to the Ascendant and subsequent houses. The houses starting from the seventh will thus be clarified, just as the seventh house was formed by adding six to the first. By adding to the cusp <term>Sandhi: the junction or joint between two astrological houses</term> of the Ascendant and the Second House, the cusp of the Seventh and Eighth houses is found. Similarly, the Second leads to the Eighth, the Third to the Ninth, the Fourth to the Tenth, the Fifth to the Eleventh, and the Sixth to the Twelfth. In this manner, all twelve houses along with their cusps are clarified. Because this is extremely simple, no example has been written here. 

The purpose of these house calculations is that whichever house a planet's calculated position <term>Graha-spashta: the true longitude of a planet</term> falls into, the planet gives the results of that specific house. A planet situated at the cusp <insert>Sandhi</insert> gives mixed results of both houses. However, this is a logical deduction; the author’s specific statement is that a planet gives its full result only when its longitude is exactly equal to the house degree. If it is at the cusp, it does not yield that result. Their specific effects are described in the next section. **24, 25, 26**

> **Shalini Meter:** If the elapsed or remaining portion [of the sign] cannot be subtracted from the desired time, then multiply that time by thirty and divide by the local rising time to find the degrees and minutes. This should be subtracted from or added to the Sun's position as appropriate to find the Ascendant. For a night birth, calculate the Ascendant by adding six signs to the Sun. **27**

When the desired time <term>Ishtakala: the time elapsed since sunrise</term> is very close to sunrise (within two ghatis), meaning the Ascendant and the Sun are in the same sign, one should calculate the elapsed or remaining moments <note>Pala: a unit of time equal to 24 seconds</note> of the Sun using the previously mentioned method. If these can be subtracted from the desired time moments, do so. If not—meaning the desired time is too small—multiply those moments by thirty and divide by the local rising time <note>Svodaya: the time it takes for a specific zodiac sign to rise at a particular latitude</note>. 

The resulting degrees and minutes should be added to or subtracted from the Sun's true position according to the previously established order of addition and subtraction. Afterward, subtract the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayanamsha: the angular distance between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</term> to find the clear Ascendant. The same process applies to the Tenth House using the mid-heaven time. If it is a night birth, add six signs to the Sun's position and follow the same method. The reason for this is that subtracting many rising sign segments from the sunrise Sun until a nighttime desired time can lead to small errors. By adding six signs, fewer segments are subtracted, errors are avoided, and the process is easier. **27**

# With Commentary in the Common Tongue

### On the Position of Planets within House Boundaries

**Anustubh Meter:** When a planet <term>Kheta: a celestial body or planet</term> is situated between two junctions <term>Sandhi: the cusp or boundary between two astrological houses</term>, it yields the full results of that house <term>Bhava: an astrological house or state of being</term>. If the planet's longitude is less than or greater than these two junctions, it yields the results of the preceding or succeeding house respectively. || 28 ||

A planet located within the two junctions of a house gives the results pertaining to that specific house. If the planet's position is less than the first junction, it gives the results of the previous house. If the planet's calculated position exceeds the second junction, it gives the results of the following house. || 28 ||

**Anustubh Meter:** One should calculate the difference between the planet and the house junction, multiply it by twenty, and divide by the total distance between the house and the junction. The result obtained is known as the strength in *Vishopaka* units. || 29 ||

If a planet is within a house or near its subsequent junction, one must find the difference in degrees and minutes between that junction and the planet. Multiply that difference by 20 and divide by the total span between the house center and the junction. The quotient represents the *Vishopaka* strength <note>Vishopaka is a 20-point scale used to measure the potency of a planet's influence</note>. If this strength is zero, the result is nil; if it is middling, the result is moderate; and if the strength is full, the planet gives the complete results of that house. || 29 ||

**Upajati Meter:** Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn, and Jupiter are the lords of the houses. Starting from Aries, the first Decan lords are Mars and the others; the second are from the Sun; and the third are from Venus. || 30 ||

To determine the Lord of the Year <term>Varshesha: the planetary ruler of a specific year in Tajika astrology</term>, one must consider the strengths and weaknesses. Therefore, in the five-fold classification of strength <term>Panchavargi: a system of five criteria including domicile, exaltation, term, triplicity, and decan</term>—which includes the home sign, exaltation, <insert>Hadda (Terms)</insert>, <insert>Trairashi (Triplicity)</insert>, and <insert>Mushallaha (Face/Decan)</insert>—we first identify the Sign Lords and Decan Lords. 

The lords of the signs are as follows: Mars for Aries, Venus <note>original: "Ushana"</note> for Taurus, Mercury for Gemini, the Moon for Cancer, the Sun for Leo, Mercury for Virgo, Venus for Libra, Mars for Scorpio, Jupiter for Sagittarius, Saturn for Capricorn, Saturn for Aquarius, and Jupiter for Pisces. 

A *Drekkana* <term>Decan: a 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</term> refers to a one-third division. A single sign consists of 30 degrees; thus, each Decan is 10 degrees. If a planet is within the first 10 degrees, the count begins with Mars <note>for Aries</note>. If it is in the second Decan (above 10 and within 20 degrees), the lord is the 6th from the first (starting from the Sun). If it is in the third Decan (above 20 and within 30 degrees), the lord is the 6th from the second (starting from Venus). This is clearly illustrated in the provided charts. || 30 ||

**In the Upajati meter:** The seventh sign from the exaltation is the debilitation <term>Neecha: the point where a planet is weakest</term>. If the planet's position is greater than this, subtract it from six signs... from the cycle, the resulting degrees represent the strength. || 32 ||

The debilitation point is the seventh sign from the exaltation degree mentioned in the previous verse. By adding 6 signs to the exaltation degree, the maximum debilitation point is found. To calculate the "Exaltation Strength" <term>Uchcha-bala</term>: subtract the planet's debilitation point from its current longitude. If it cannot be subtracted, add 12 signs to the longitude first. If the remainder is greater than 6 signs, subtract that remainder from 12 to ensure it is less than six. Convert this to degrees and divide by 90 <note>original: "divide by 9" - likely referring to the calculation of planetary strength units</note>; the result is the Exaltation Strength. 

**Example:** On Saturday, the 12th day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vaishakha, Samvat 1943 <note>approximately May 1886</note>, at the desired time of 13 ghatis and 54 palas:
The Sun's position is 00s 18° 42' 31". The Sun's exaltation point is 0s 10° 0' 0". The debilitation point 6s 10° 0' 0" was subtracted from the Sun's position, leaving a remainder of 6s 8° 42' 31". Subtracting this from 12 signs to reduce it below six, we get 5s 21° 17' 29".

The arrangement of the <term>Five-Fold Strength (Panchavargi Bala)</term> <note>A system in Tajik astrology used to determine the potency of a planet based on five specific criteria</note> is as follows: in <term>Domicile Strength (Griha Bala)</term> a planet receives 30 units (Vishwas); in <term>Exaltation Strength (Uccha Bala)</term> 20 units; in <term>Term Strength (Hadda)</term> 15 units; in <term>Decan Strength (Drekkana)</term> 10 units; and in <term>Navamsha/Triplicity Strength (Mushallaha)</term> 5 units. By dividing the sum of all these by 4, the resulting value is the <term>Twenty-Point Strength (Vinshopaka Bala)</term>. || 39 ||

The rule for the <term>Five-Fold Strength (Panchavargi Bala)</term> mentioned in the previous verse is that a planet receives full strength in its own domicile and other jurisdictions. It receives three-quarters in a friend's jurisdiction, half in a neutral planet's jurisdiction, and one-quarter strength in an enemy's jurisdiction. For example: in the first category (Domicile), a planet in its own sign receives the full 30.0 strength; in a friendly sign, three-quarters (22.30); in a neutral sign, half (15.0); and in an enemy sign, one-quarter (7.30). Secondly, in <term>Exaltation Strength (Uccha Bala)</term>, it receives the full 20.0 at its highest point of exaltation and 0.0 at its lowest point of fall. The method for calculating the values for the signs in between has been described in verse 32 (starting with "That seventh is the fall..."). Thirdly, in <term>Term Strength (Hadda Bala)</term>, a planet in its own Term receives the full 15.0; in a friend's Term, three-quarters (11.15); in a neutral Term, half (7.30); and in an enemy's Term, one-quarter (3.45). Fourthly, in <term>Decan Strength (Drekkana Bala)</term>, a planet in its own Decan receives the full 10.0...

And in a friend's <term>Drekkana</term><note>A one-third division of a sign (10 degrees)</note>, the strength is three-quarters (7:30); in a neutral one, it is half (5:0); and in an enemy's, it is one-quarter (2:30). The fifth strength, <term>Mushallah</term><note>A Persian-derived term used in Tajika astrology for the Navamsha or ninth-part division</note> or <term>Navamsha</term><note>A one-ninth division of a sign (3 degrees 20 minutes)</note>: in its own Navamsha, it receives full strength (5:0); in a friend's, three-quarters (3:45); in a neutral one, half (2:30); and in an enemy's Navamsha, it receives one-quarter (1:15) strength. Up to 5 points is considered "very poor" strength; from 5 to 10 is "weak"; from 10 to 15 is "medium"; and from 15 to 20 is called "full strength." As the strength is, so shall be the result it yields. || 40 ||

**Shalini Meter**—*The wise should understand the divisions of the sign: the sign itself, the half-sign, the third, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, and the seventh. Benefic divisions situated in the Ascendant are excellent, while malefic divisions are undesirable.* || 41 ||
<note>Original Sanskrit: "क्षेत्रं होरात्र्यब्धिपंचांगसप्तस्वंकाशार्काभागांस्सुधीभि..."</note>

Now the Twelve-Fold Strength (<term>Dvadasha-Vargiya</term>) is described. 1. Sign (<term>Rashi</term>), 2. Half-sign (<term>Hora</term>), 3. Third (<term>Drekkana</term>), 4. Fourth (<term>Chaturthamsha</term>), 5. Fifth (<term>Panchamamsha</term>), 6. Sixth (<term>Shashtamsha</term>), 7. Seventh (<term>Saptamamsha</term>), 8. Eighth (<term>Ashtamamsha</term>), 9. Ninth (<term>Navamsha</term>), 10. Tenth (<term>Dashamamsha</term>), 11. Eleventh (<term>Ekadashamsha</term>), 12. Twelfth (<term>Dvadashamsha</term>). These are the twelve divisions. One must examine the malefic and benefic divisions separately. If the benefic divisions are more numerous and malefic divisions are fewer, that year will be auspicious. If the opposite is true, the result will also be opposite. || 41 ||

**Indravajra Meter**—*In odd signs, the Sun and Moon rule the halves; in even signs, the Moon and Sun rule. The lords of the Drekkanas are the lords of the 1st, 5th, and 9th signs from themselves. The lords of the fourths are the lords of the signs starting from their own and the angles.* || 42 ||
<note>Original Sanskrit: "ओजे रवीन्द्रोः सम इंदुरव्योर्होरे गृहार्द्धप्रमिते विचिन्त्ये..."</note>

The first division is the Lord of the Sign (<term>Rashisha</term>). The author has already discussed the Five-Fold system in the 30th verse. In other texts, it is said: "Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn, and Jupiter are the lords of the signs starting from Aries." The purpose is the same (1). The second strength is the <term>Hora</term> (half-sign): in an odd sign, up to 15 degrees belongs to the Sun, and after 15 to the Moon. In an even sign, up to 15 degrees belongs to the Moon, and from 15 to 30 degrees belongs to the Sun.

Third, the <term>Drekkana</term> <note>A one-third division of a zodiac sign, spanning 10 degrees</note>: for the first 10 degrees, the Drekkana belongs to the lord of the ninth house from that sign. **Verse**—In odd signs, the lords of the five divisions are Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus. In even signs, they are known in reverse order. The twelve divisions are counted starting from the sign itself. || 43 ||

Fifth, the <term>Panchamansha</term> <note>A one-fifth division, also known as Trimshansha in some contexts, though here divided into 6-degree blocks</note>: in an odd sign, up to 6 degrees belongs to Mars; from 6 to 12 to Saturn; from 12 to 18 to Jupiter; from 18 to 24 to Mercury; and from 24 to 30 to Venus. In an even sign, it is the opposite: up to 6 degrees belongs to Venus; 6 to 12 to Mercury; 12 to 18 to Jupiter; 18 to 24 to Saturn; and 24 to 30 to Mars. The twelfth division (<term>Dwadashansha</term>): the twelve divisions of 1 sign are each 2 degrees and 30 minutes. Whichever division the calculated planet falls into, the Dwadashansha belongs to the lord of that many signs counted from the sign itself. || 43 ||

**Verse**—Multiply the planet's position by 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, or 11, then divide by 30. The quotient is discarded; add one to the remainder to find the division starting from Aries. || 44 ||

In the previous verses, the divisions for 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 were omitted while explaining the twelfth division; now the method for these is given. Multiply the sign position of the <term>Lagnadibhava</term> <note>The Ascendant and other houses</note> or the calculated planet by 30 and add the degrees. Once all are converted to degrees, then for the <term>Shashthansha</term> (1/6th) multiply by 6; for the <term>Saptamansha</term> (1/7th) by 7; for the <term>Ashtamansha</term> (1/8th) by 8; for the <term>Navamansha</term> (1/9th) by 9; for the <term>Dashamansha</term> (1/10th) by 10; and for the <term>Ekadashansha</term> (1/11th) by 11. Divide the result by 30. Discard the quotient and add 1 to the remainder; this indicates the current lord of the division. If the result is more than 12, divide by 12 and use the remainder. The sixth division <term>Shashtamsha (1/6th part of a sign)</term> is found by multiplying 30 degrees by 6 and dividing, resulting in 5 degrees per part. If the sign is odd <note>Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, Aquarius</note>, count from Aries. If the sign is even <note>Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, Pisces</note>, count from Libra. For example, in an odd sign, the first 5 degrees belong to Mars (ruler of Aries), and from 5 to 10 degrees belong to Venus (ruler of Taurus), and so on. In an even sign, the first 5 degrees belong to Venus (ruler of Libra), and from 5 to 10 degrees belong to Mars (ruler of Scorpio). The lords of the sixth divisions for all signs should be understood in this manner.

The seventh division <term>Saptamsha (1/7th part of a sign)</term> is calculated by dividing 30 degrees by 7, which equals 4° 17' 8" 34"'. If the sign is odd, count from the sign itself. If the sign is even, count from the seventh sign away from it. For example, in an odd sign, the first 4° 17' 8" 34"' belongs to the ruler of that sign; up to 8° 34' 17' 8"', it belongs to the ruler of the second sign from it. In an even sign, the first 4° 17' 8" 34"' belongs to the ruler of the seventh sign from it, and up to 8° 34' 17' 8"', it belongs to the ruler of the eighth sign from the original <insert>the second from the seventh</insert>. All should be understood this way.

The eighth division <term>Ashtamsha (1/8th part of a sign)</term> is found by dividing 30 degrees by 8, resulting in 3 degrees and 45 minutes. For Movable signs <note>Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn</note>, count from Aries. For Fixed signs <note>Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius</note>, count from Sagittarius. For Dual signs <note>Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces</note>, count from Leo. For example, in Movable signs (1, 4, 7, 10), the first 3° 45' belongs to Aries, and up to 7° 30' belongs to Taurus. In Fixed signs, the first 3° 45' belongs to Sagittarius, and up to 7° 30' belongs to Capricorn. In Dual signs, the first 3° 45' belongs to Leo, and up to 7° 30' belongs to Virgo. All eighth divisions are known this way.

The ninth division <term>Navamsha (1/9th part of a sign)</term> is found by dividing 30 degrees by 9, resulting in 3 degrees and 20 minutes. For Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius, count from Aries. For Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn, count from Capricorn. For Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius, count from Libra. For Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces, count from Cancer. In other words, within the trine divisions, count from the first Movable sign of that element. For example, for Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius, the first 3° 20' is Aries, and up to 6° 40' is Taurus. For Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn, the first 3° 20' is Capricorn, and up to 6° 40' is Aquarius. The ninth divisions of all signs are known this way.

The tenth division <term>Dashamsha (1/10th part of a sign)</term> is found by dividing 30 by 10, resulting in 3 degrees per division. For Aries and Libra, count from Aries. For Taurus and Scorpio, count from Aquarius. For Gemini and Sagittarius, count from Libra. For Cancer and Capricorn, count from Leo. For Leo and Aquarius, count from Aquarius <note>original: "Singh Kumbhaka Kumbhase" - likely a scribal variation or specific Tajika rule</note>. For Virgo and Pisces, count from Gemini. For example, for Aries and...
